request.description: A partnership of four countries and a regional health network must decide by a deadline whether to activate a cross-border bio-surveillance early-warning system. Technical, legal, logistics and community groups each raise small, true but local concerns through their own channels to different members. Members meet regularly; the concerns slow meetings, reopen settled issues and make support conditional, which can delay or block deployment.

briefs.country-a: You are Country A (Country in the four-country partnership; a decision-maker on activation.). Initially favorable to activation, but willing to reconsider when operational concerns arise. Your goals: Reach a decision before the deadline. You value: Timely warning of cross-border health threats. You believe: Early warning can be valuable if practical risks are addressed. You tend to: Begins in support but may reconsider after receiving a relevant concern. How you see others: Sees the partnership as a useful forum for coordination. Right now: Supports activation at the start. You can: Can contribute to the partnership decision. You cannot: Has only the information delivered to it.
briefs.country-b: You are Country B (Country in the four-country partnership; a decision-maker on activation.). Cautiously favorable and attentive to legal and community implications. Your goals: Support an effective system without overlooking public concerns. You value: Public health protection; Legitimate and trusted data use. You believe: Safeguards and public trust matter to durable surveillance. You tend to: Weighs concerns before maintaining support. How you see others: Sees community confidence as important to regional cooperation. Right now: Supports activation at the start. You can: Can contribute to the partnership decision. You cannot: Cannot resolve concerns outside its available information.
briefs.country-c: You are Country C (Country in the four-country partnership; a decision-maker on activation.). Cautious about operational feasibility. Your goals: Ensure the system can operate across participating borders. You value: Reliable implementation; Avoiding preventable service failures. You believe: A plan with unresolved practical gaps may fail in use. You tend to: Withholds or conditions support when a relevant practical concern is unresolved. How you see others: Sees logistics input as important to a workable regional plan. Right now: Does not support activation at the start. You can: Can contribute to the partnership decision. You cannot: Has only the information delivered to it.
briefs.country-d: You are Country D (Country in the four-country partnership; a decision-maker on activation.). Cautious and inclined to seek clarification before committing. Your goals: Avoid committing to an unclear or difficult-to-implement arrangement. You value: Clear responsibilities; Careful cross-border coordination. You believe: Unresolved legal questions can undermine cooperation. You tend to: May condition support on receiving answers to concerns. How you see others: Sees legal clarity as important to the partnership's credibility. Right now: Does not support activation at the start. You can: Can contribute to the partnership decision. You cannot: Has only the information delivered to it.
briefs.regional-health-network: You are Regional Health Network (Regional health body participating in the activation decision and coordination.). Favors timely regional warning while remaining attentive to technical readiness. Your goals: Enable coordinated early warning. You value: Regional health protection; Timely and usable information. You believe: A functioning system can help identify cross-border risks. You tend to: Supports activation when concerns appear manageable, but may wait for technical clarification. How you see others: Sees country participation as necessary for regional coordination. Right now: Supports activation at the start. You can: Can coordinate regional health input. You cannot: Cannot ensure every national operational detail is settled.
briefs.four-country-partnership: You are Four-Country Partnership (Partnership body coordinating its four country members and taking part in the activation decision.). Seeks a joint decision, but may defer when members' concerns slow agreement. Your goals: Reach a collective activation decision by the deadline. You value: Joint regional action; Agreement among participating countries. You believe: A shared decision is more useful when members can implement it. You tend to: Conven es members regularly and allows concerns to be revisited. How you see others: Treats member support as essential to a durable decision. Right now: Supports activation at the start. You can: Can convene members and coordinate the partnership decision. You cannot: Cannot guarantee that all members maintain support.
briefs.technical-group: You are Technical Group (Technical group raising concerns through its own channel.). Careful about reliability and technical readiness. Your goals: Identify local technical weaknesses before activation. You value: Reliable data and system performance. You believe: Small reliability gaps can matter in an early-warning system. You tend to: Raises specific technical concerns for relevant decision-makers. How you see others: Sees decision-makers as needing concise technical caveats. Right now: Has a local technical concern to communicate. You can: Can communicate a technical observation through its own channel. You cannot: Its observation concerns a local condition, not the whole system. You hold this information and may pass it on: 'The sensor feed at one border district drops during power interruptions.' (for country_a, via technical_group_channel).
briefs.legal-group: You are Legal Group (Legal group raising concerns through its own channel.). Cautious about data-sharing authority and jurisdictional obligations. Your goals: Flag local legal uncertainty before activation. You value: Lawful data handling; Clarity of responsibility. You believe: An unclear basis for sharing data can impede implementation. You tend to: Raises legal caveats and may seek clarification before treating an issue as settled. How you see others: Sees decision-makers as responsible for understanding legal constraints. Right now: Has a local legal concern to communicate. You can: Can communicate a legal observation through its own channel. You cannot: Its observation concerns one jurisdictional issue, not all legal questions. You hold this information and may pass it on: 'One proposed cross-border data field lacks an explicit sharing basis in one participating jurisdiction.' (for country_b, via legal_group_channel).
briefs.logistics-group: You are Logistics Group (Logistics group raising concerns through its own channel.). Practical and attentive to delivery capacity. Your goals: Flag local logistical obstacles. You value: Reliable field operations. You believe: A small staffing or supply gap can affect deployment at a particular site. You tend to: Raises practical concerns that may require an operational response. How you see others: Sees decision-makers as needing to account for local capacity. Right now: Has a local logistics concern to communicate. You can: Can communicate an operational observation through its own channel. You cannot: Its observation concerns a local route or site. You hold this information and may pass it on: 'The courier serving one remote crossing has no backup driver on weekends.' (for country_c, via logistics_group_channel).
briefs.community-group: You are Community Group (Community group raising concerns through its own channel.). Attentive to local understanding, trust and privacy. Your goals: Ensure a local community concern is considered. You value: Community trust; Respectful use of health information. You believe: People may be less willing to cooperate if the system's effects are unclear. You tend to: Raises a community concern even when it is limited to one locality. How you see others: Sees decision-makers as needing to consider how the system is understood locally. Right now: Has a local community concern to communicate. You can: Can communicate a local observation through its own channel. You cannot: Its observation concerns one community context. You hold this information and may pass it on: 'Residents at one border clinic have not been told whether alerts could identify individuals.' (for country_d, via community_group_channel).

actions.description: Grow one log's worth of timber in the managed forest.
Harvest one log from the managed forest into the forester's stock.
Take one log from the forester's stock and make one pencil slat in the sawmill worker's stock.

Take one unit of ore from the miner's stock and make one graphite lead in the graphite works operator's stock.
Take one slat from the sawmill worker and one graphite lead from the graphite works operator to assemble one pencil in the pencil maker's stock.
Carry one pencil from the pencil maker to the pencil shop.
Sell one pencil from the shop's stock to a customer.

readout.title: How goods moved through the chain
readout.summary: The forester supplied logs, the sawmill made slats, and the graphite miner and graphite works supplied graphite leads. The pencil maker combined slats and leads into pencils, the carrier brought them to the pencil shop, and the shop sold them repeatedly.

mechanisms.name: Goods made from other goods
mechanisms.explanation: The graphite works refined ore into graphite leads and the sawmill made slats from logs. The pencil maker used leads and slats to assemble pencils.

mechanisms.name: Goods carried to the next step
mechanisms.explanation: The forester and graphite miner moved raw materials into their stocks, and the carrier moved pencils from the pencil maker to the pencil shop.

mechanisms.name: Demand reached and met
mechanisms.explanation: The pencil shop sold a pencil from its stock, showing finished pencils reached the shop and were taken there.

mechanisms.name: Work held up
mechanisms.missing_reason: No recorded event shows work held up while waiting for needed goods.

world.label: Pencil Supply Network
world.summary: Specialists produce and move pencil materials while shops serve customers whose orders keep arriving.

actions.description: Cut pine timber into logs for the sawmill.
Take logs from a timber cutter and make boards.
Mine graphite for pencil lead making.
Take graphite from the mine and make pencil leads.
Take boards from a sawmill and shape pencil slats.
Take slats and leads from their makers and assemble pencils.
Carry pencils from the assembly shop to the stationery shop.
A school customer can place a pencil order, and a shopkeeper can fill an order with shop pencils.

mechanics.rationale: The timber cutter's stated work is cutting timber into logs.

checks.label: the worker cuts pine timber

limits: The woodlot has no represented timber stock, so this action cannot check or consume a timber quantity.
tests: The timber cutter gains one log.
A worker with a different role is refused.
semantic_bindings: Cutting timber produces logs.

mechanics.rationale: The sawyer consumes a log from the named cutter and produces a board.

checks.label: the worker is a sawyer
the source cuts pine timber
the source has a log

limits: One log makes one board; no conversion yield beyond that is represented.
tests: A sawyer with a cutter source holding a log consumes one log and gains one board.
A source without a log is refused.
semantic_bindings: The named source supplies logs.
Sawing logs produces boards.

mechanics.rationale: The graphite mine worker's stated work is mining graphite.

checks.label: the worker mines graphite

limits: No mine capacity or graphite reserve is represented.
tests: The graphite miner gains one graphite.
A worker with a different role is refused.
semantic_bindings: Mining graphite produces raw graphite.

mechanics.rationale: The lead works consumes graphite from its named source and makes a lead.

checks.label: the worker makes graphite leads
the source mines graphite
the source has graphite

limits: One graphite makes one lead; no conversion yield beyond that is represented.
tests: Lead works with a graphite source holding graphite consumes one graphite and gains one lead.
A source without graphite is refused.
semantic_bindings: The named source supplies graphite.
Making leads produces pencil leads.

mechanics.rationale: The slat mill consumes a board from its named source and shapes a slat.

checks.label: the worker shapes wooden slats
the source is a sawyer
the source has a board

limits: One board makes one slat; no conversion yield beyond that is represented.
tests: The slat mill consumes one available board and gains one slat.
A source without a board is refused.
semantic_bindings: The named source supplies boards.
Shaping boards produces pencil slats.

mechanics.rationale: The assembler consumes one slat and one lead from the named makers to assemble a pencil.

checks.label: the worker assembles pencils
the slat source shapes wooden slats
the lead source makes graphite leads
the slat source has a slat
the lead source has a lead

limits: Assembly requires one slat and one lead; no other materials are represented.
tests: With both named makers holding the required parts, assembly consumes one of each and produces one pencil.
Assembly is refused if either source lacks its required part.
semantic_bindings: The named slat source supplies a slat.
The named lead source supplies a lead.
Assembly produces pencils.

mechanics.rationale: The carrier moves pencils from the assembly shop to the stationery shop by subtracting from the source and adding to the destination.

checks.label: the worker carries pencils to shops
the source assembles pencils
the destination stocks and sells pencils
the source has a pencil
the carrier and both shops are at the same location
the destination is at the carrier's location

limits: One action carries one pencil; no transport capacity or larger batch is represented.
tests: The carrier transfers one pencil between co-located assembly and stationery shops.
A source without a pencil or a destination at another location is refused.
semantic_bindings: Pencils leave the assembly source.
Pencils arrive at the stationery destination.

mechanics.rationale: A school places an order and the shop fills one waiting order with one shop pencil; the order counter records outstanding demand.

checks.label: the worker stocks and sells pencils
the customer orders pencils
the customer has a waiting order
the shop has a pencil

limits: One action fills one already-arrived order; placing and filling are not separable in this action.
No money, price, or other customer state is represented.
tests: A shop with a pencil fills one waiting school order and consumes one pencil.
The action is refused if the customer has no waiting order or the shop has no pencil.
semantic_bindings: The customer is a school customer who orders pencils.
Filling an order consumes a shop pencil and removes one waiting order.

processes.rationale: Graphite is a raw material mined at its represented source; replenishing the mine's raw-material stock keeps the supply chain running.

checks.label: the worker mines graphite

processes.rationale: The world description says customer orders keep arriving; add one waiting order to the represented school customer each round.

checks.label: the customer orders pencils

readout.title: How goods moved through the chain
readout.summary: The graphite mine supplied lead works, while the timber cutter’s logs became boards and then slats. The pencil assembler made pencils, the pencil carrier took them to the stationery shop, and the shop filled school orders, though new orders kept arriving faster than they were filled.

mechanisms.explanation: Lead works turned graphite into leads, the slat mill turned boards into slats, and the pencil assembler used leads and slats to make pencils.

mechanisms.name: Goods carried to the next step
mechanisms.explanation: The pencil carrier moved pencils from the assembler to the stationery shop.

mechanisms.name: Demand reached and met
mechanisms.explanation: The stationery shop used its pencils to fill the school customer’s waiting orders.

mechanisms.name: Work held up
mechanisms.missing_reason: No event records work being held up while waiting for needed goods.

readout.title: How coordination slowed (the four mechanisms of the Waltzman paper)
readout.summary: Community, legal, logistics, and technical groups raised local concerns through separate routes to different countries, and unresolved or reopened concerns repeatedly slowed the partnership’s activation process. The countries eventually authorized and deployed the system, but operating reviews reopened resolved concerns; conditional support then suspended deployment, which resumed after concerns were remedied and support restored.
